intro: By the end of sixth grade, you should be able to read and understand stories, plays, and poems written at a sixth to eighth grade level. This skill brings together everything else: following the plot, understanding characters, noticing the author's craft, and drawing conclusions. These exercises give you a passage and ask a mix of straightforward and deeper questions.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The morning of the regional spelling bee, Priya could barely eat her breakfast. She had studied for months, filling three notebooks with words and their origins. Her father drove her to the auditorium in silence, sensing she needed the quiet. When her turn came, the announcer gave her the word 'mnemonic.' Priya closed her eyes. She pictured the page in her notebook where she had written it, the small drawing she had made of a brain tied with a string. Slowly, letter by letter, she spelled it correctly. She did not win the whole competition, but as she walked off the stage, her father was already standing, clapping before anyone else had moved.

How does Priya feel at the beginning of the passage, and what detail shows this?

steps: Look for clues about Priya's emotional state in the opening.
The passage says she 'could barely eat her breakfast,' a physical sign of nervousness.
Months of study also show how much the bee mattered to her.
solution.answer: Priya feels very nervous at the beginning. The detail that she 'could barely eat her breakfast' shows her anxiety, and the fact that she had studied for months filling three notebooks shows how much the competition meant to her.

steps: Notice what the father does rather than what he says.
He drives in silence, 'sensing she needed the quiet,' showing he understands her.

solution.answer: You can infer that Priya and her father have a close, understanding relationship. He senses she needs silence and gives it to her, and he is the first to stand and clap, showing he is proud of her effort regardless of whether she won.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The lighthouse on Gull Point had stood empty for years. The village children dared one another to climb its rusted stairs, but none ever did, until the summer Wen arrived from the city. Bored and friendless, she pushed open the creaking door one foggy afternoon. Inside, dust covered everything, but on the top floor she found a logbook left by the last keeper. Page after page recorded the weather, the ships, and small notes: 'Saw a whale today.' 'The Henderson boy waved from his boat.' Wen read until the light faded. The keeper had been alone too, she realized, but he had filled his days by paying attention to the world around him. She decided she would try the same.

What does Wen discover in the lighthouse, and why is it important to her?

steps: Identify the object she finds on the top floor.
She finds the last keeper's logbook full of small observations.
Reading it changes how she thinks about being alone.
solution.answer: Wen discovers the last keeper's logbook, filled with notes about the weather, ships, and small daily sights. It is important because it shows her that the keeper, who was also alone, filled his days by paying close attention to the world, and she decides to do the same.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Marcus had always been the slowest runner in his class, the one picked last, the one who finished long after everyone else. So when the gym teacher announced a charity walkathon, Marcus signed up without telling anyone. Walking, it turned out, was something he could do for hours. While the fast runners burned out after a few laps, Marcus kept a steady pace, lap after lap, long into the afternoon. By the end of the day he had walked more miles than anyone, raising the most money for the shelter. The fast kids had forgotten there was more than one way to be good at something. Marcus had not.

What is the central message of the passage about Marcus?

steps: Consider what Marcus succeeds at and how.
He is slow at running but excellent at steady, long-distance walking.
The last lines point to the message directly.
solution.answer: The central message is that there is more than one way to be good at something. Marcus, the slowest runner, discovers that his steady pace makes him excellent at long-distance walking, succeeding where the fast runners burn out. The passage suggests that everyone has their own strengths.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Grandmother's hands were not graceful anymore. They trembled as she rolled the dough, and flour dusted her sleeves where it never used to. But Sofia watched closely, the way she had every winter since she was small, as those shaking hands shaped the holiday bread into perfect braids. 'Your turn,' Grandmother said, sliding the bowl across the table. Sofia's hands were steady but clumsy; her braid came out lumpy and uneven. 'It is perfect,' Grandmother said. Sofia started to argue, then saw her grandmother's eyes, and understood that 'perfect' had never been about the bread at all.

What does Grandmother mean when she says the lumpy bread is 'perfect,' and how do you know?

steps: Her words seem to contradict the description of the bread.
Sofia looks at her grandmother's eyes and understands.
The final line explains that 'perfect' was 'never about the bread at all.'
solution.answer: Grandmother means that the value of the moment is in Sofia learning the family tradition and spending time together, not in the bread itself. We know because the passage says Sofia 'understood that perfect had never been about the bread at all,' showing the word refers to the shared experience.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The new boy, Eli, did not speak for the first two weeks. The other students decided he was unfriendly and left him alone. But Talia noticed that he always sat near the window, sketching in a worn notebook, and that his drawings were extraordinary, full of imaginary cities and winged machines. One day she sat down across from him and slid her own sketchbook over. He looked at it, then at her, and turned to a fresh page. Without a word, they began to draw the same city together, each adding to the other's lines. Sometimes, Talia thought, friendship did not need a single spoken word to begin.

Why do the other students think Eli is unfriendly, and why are they mistaken?
items.hint: Consider what the students notice versus what they fail to notice.

steps: The students judge Eli because he does not speak for two weeks.
They never look closer at what he is doing, his extraordinary drawings.
Talia's experience shows he was open to connection all along.
solution.answer: The other students think Eli is unfriendly because he does not speak for the first two weeks, so they assume the worst and leave him alone. They are mistaken because they never look closer; Talia discovers his remarkable drawings and his willingness to connect when she simply shares her own sketchbook.
